newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia communists mark failed anti-Yeltsin revolt.
newsitem.headline: Russia communists mark failed anti-Yeltsin revolt.

text.p: Thousands of people, mainly hardline communists and nationalists, marched through central Moscow on Friday to commemorate an uprising crushed three years ago by tanks and troops loyal to President Boris Yeltsin.

Led by Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, the sombre crowd of mostly older Russians carried red Soviet flags, portraits of people killed in the revolt and banners bearing slogans like "No forgiveness for the butchers".
On October 4 1993 Yeltsin sent in tanks and troops to batter his hardline opponents inside the White House parliament into submission after weeks of tense confrontation.
About 140 people died in the "October events" during which Russia seemed to totter on the brink of civil war.
"Let all those in power remember that nobody has the right to dissolve and shoot at a legitimately elected body and to pit the army against the people," Zyuganov told reporters on Friday.
"Only then will we have reconciliation," he said.
At the time Yeltsin said the storming of parliament, witnessed by millions live on television, was necessary to prevent communists and neo-fascists seizing power.
His tanks moved in only after a bloody assault by anti-Yeltsin forces on Moscow's Ostankino television centre.
The showdown with the legislature, where rebel deputies and their supporters were holed up, followed a two-year stand-off in which Yeltsin accused it of blocking his reforms.
"They (Yeltsin and his government) are my enemies, I hate them. I can't bear to look at them," said Galina Nikitina, a middle-aged woman clutching a single rose.
"I consider Yeltsin a traitor. I support the old Soviet constitution," she told Reuters.
She said she had helped defend the White House in 1993. "We were like one big family united in a good cause. We helped each other, we shared everything till the fighting began."

"You see what has happened to Russia since then?" said Volodya, a 37-year-old manual worker. "Expensive restaurants keep opening up where only foreigners and our mafia can afford to go. They chase ordinary Russians away from such places."

The marchers wound their way past a huge McDonald's fast food chain -- where prices are still discouragingly high for many ordinary people -- and several stylish bars and private clubs frequented by the new class of affluent Russians.
Businessman Alexander Tkachenko did not share the marchers' view of events back in 1993.
"It was very scary. It really looked like the communists were about to take power again," he said.

"Before the army went in armed rebels seemed to take over central Moscow and they had crazed looks on their faces. Yet when you went down into the Metro people were going about their usual business, oblivious to the drama going on above them."
"It all felt unreal. The forces of law and order had to intervene," he added.

Reflecting the diverse political beliefs of the loose anti-Yeltsin coalition, old-style communists nostalgic for the Soviet era mingled with young ultra-nationalists in combat gear and bearded Russian Orthodox priests.

Zyuganov ran unsuccessfully against Yeltsin in this summer's presidential election as the candidate of the Bloc of National-Patriotic Forces -- a catch-all coalition comprising Bolsheviks, nationalists, agrarians and some social democrats.
Since its electoral defeat the opposition has recovered some of its confidence, with Zyuganov spearheading calls for the ailing Yeltsin to resign.
The 65-year-old Kremlin leader, who slipped out of the public eye days before his election victory, is in hospital preparing for heart bypass surgery in the next month or two.
However under the new constitution introduced after Yeltsin's showdown with parliament the president has sweeping powers that mean the opposition has little hope of forcing him into early retirement.
